media.author: Petrus Apianus (Peter Apian), with Georg Apian; printed, hand-coloured and assembled in the Apians' workshop
media.source: National Library of Poland (Polona, object 149346690), via Wikimedia Commons; public domain
media.note: The instrument cut off its page by distance from the paper's own colour. The turning paper disc (and its two tabs, CAPVT and CAVDA, with the shadows they cast on the mater) cut along its own hand-cut edge, measured angle by angle about the pin; its colour solved so that the restored mater under it plus the disc equals the scan at rest. Under each tab the mater's zodiac ring was restored from the same printed sign 60 or 120 degrees round (the white signs repeat their numerals and checker), registered on the ring either side, its seams on printed cell rules; the gap between the disc and the ring from the same gap a sector along. Scaled to 1600 px wide. Nothing drawn.

    Peter Apian printed the Astronomicum Caesareum in Ingolstadt in 1540 for the emperor Charles V, and coloured, cut and assembled its paper instruments in his own workshop. On this one a paper disc, tied at its centre, turns over the zodiac. Its dragon's head and tail mark the two points where the moon's path crosses the sun's; set the head against the year, read the moon's latitude off the arcs.

    The nodes go backwards through the signs, one full turn in eighteen and a half years. Here the turn is the work: a value turns the disc that far, and at the end the head is home where it was printed.

# dragon-volvelle A loader / progress indicator that is Peter Apian's lunar dragon volvelle, from the *Astronomicum Caesareum* (Ingolstadt, 1540). The hand-coloured woodcut lies on the page, cut to its printed outline, and its own paper disc turns on its centre over the printed zodiac, the way the book's reader turned it. With a value, the disc has turned through that share of a full turn: the dragon's head (the tab CAPVT) goes back through the signs, the way the moon's node does, and at 100% it is home where it was printed. With no value, the disc keeps going round slowly. While it waits it can be handled: take the disc and turn it, and when you let go the work takes it back. At rest it is the plate, pixel for pixel: what you are looking at is the ``. The control is a real ``. ```html

``` Drive it by setting the `` as you normally would (`bar.value = n`, or `bar.removeAttribute('value')` for indeterminate). The component watches the element. Or use the API: ```js import { dragonVolvelle } from './dragon-volvelle.js'; const v = dragonVolvelle(root, { turn: 40 }); v.value = .4; // 40%: the disc goes 144 degrees back through the signs v.value = null; // indeterminate: it goes round v.done(); // 100%: home root.addEventListener('dragon-volvelle:change', (e) => e.detail.value); root.addEventListener('dragon-volvelle:done', () => {}); root.addEventListener('dragon-volvelle:turned', (e) => e.detail.angle); // a hand let go of it v(); // destroy: removes the canvas, live region, listeners and loop; leaves the plain markup ``` If the value goes down (a new job), the disc carries on forwards from wherever it is, so it never runs backwards. Without JS it is the plate and a native `` (the CSS hides the bar only once the script has started). ## In life, and here | In life | Here | |---|---| | Apian printed the plates from woodblocks, had them coloured, and cut and assembled the paper instruments in his own workshop. The disc is tied at its centre and turns over the mater, the printed base. | The scan's own disc is cut along its own hand-cut edge, which is measured angle by angle (radius 1309 to 1319 px at 3840 px), so it turns with its real, slightly irregular outline. It turns about the centre printed on the disc, fitted to its rules to 0.4 px. | | The disc carries the dragon, two tabs at its rim (CAPVT, the ascending node, and CAVDA, the descending node), rings of year marks, and the arched latitude scales. The reader set CAPVT against the node's longitude on the mater's zodiac, from the tables, and read the moon's latitude off the arcs. | The two tabs are part of the disc, and so are the small shadows they cast on the mater. Under them, the mater's zodiac ring is restored from the same printed sign 60 or 120 degrees round (the white signs repeat their numerals and checker), registered on the ring either side, with its seams on printed cell rules. Nothing is drawn. | | The moon's nodes regress: they go backwards through the signs, one full turn in about 18.6 years. | The disc turns clockwise on the page, which is backwards through the signs (they run counter-clockwise on this mater). A value turns it through that share of one full turn, and at 100% CAPVT is back on Scorpio, where it was printed. With no value it goes round once every 40 seconds. | | You turned it by hand. | You still can. A drag on the disc or a tab turns it about the pin. Let go and a critically damped spring takes it back to the value (or friction brings it back to its slow turn). The work never turns it faster than 100 degrees a second, and a hand can turn it at any speed. | Simplified, and why: - The real volvelle has a thread from the centre for reading across the scales. This copy's thread is gone, so it is not here either. - The disc is a flat sheet. The real paper sits a fraction of a millimetre above the mater. Only the tabs' small cast shadows show that, and they turn with the tabs. ## How it was cut (offline, `tools/`) Python, `./tools/run.sh .py`. The source goes in `tools/engine/jobs/dragon-volvelle-src/` (see `credits.json`). 1. `geometry.py`: the printed centre (circles fitted to the disc's own rules), the paper edge per quarter degree, the zodiac's inner rule and the rough tab sectors. 2. `cut.py`: the disc's alpha, with the edge carried across the tabs. The tabs are found by their yellow paper, and their convex hulls are drawn antialiased. Under each tab, the ring inside the checker's outer rule comes from the same sign a third or a sixth of the way round, in polar coordinates about the mater, registered per side (angle and radius, about 0.15 rms). Its tone comes from the bare paper either side, and its sector's edges are snapped to printed cell rules. The gap between the disc and the ring comes from the same gap a sector along, at the same radius. In the blank strip before the sign names, the tab's soft shadow is divided out. The shadow layer is how much darker the scan is than the restored mater, so it travels with its tab. The disc's colour is solved so that `base·(1−a) + F·a = scan`. 3. `export.py`: the instrument is cut off its page by Lab distance from the paper's own colour (filled, opened, 1 px feather), at 1600 px wide. `ring.webp` is the restored mater in the annulus the turning disc can uncover. `disc.webp` is the disc, its tabs and their shadows, as a square about the pin. `volvelle.json` holds the geometry. ## Runtime Canvas 2D, about 300 lines, no libraries. At its size the canvas caches a base once (the plate, with the restored ring over it) and the disc resampled once to device pixels, so each frame is one blit plus one rotated blit. The loop runs only while the disc moves, or while it goes round indeterminately and is on screen in a visible tab. At rest the canvas is hidden and the `` shows. Fixed 240 Hz substeps keep the spring stable at any frame rate. `v.hold(true)` stops the loop and `v.advance(seconds)` steps it exactly (for screenshots). ## Options | Option | Attribute | Default | | |---|---|---|---| | `turn` | `data-turn` | `40` | Seconds per turn while indeterminate. | | `speed` | `data-speed` | `100` | The most degrees a second the work turns it (a hand can turn it faster). | | `touch` | `data-touch` | `true` | `false`: look-only. | | `src` | `data-src` | `volvelle.json` beside the image | Geometry; `ring.webp` and `disc.webp` sit beside it. | | `doneText` | `data-done-text` | `Done.` | What the live region says at 100%. | | | `data-busy` on `.dv-readout` | | Words shown while indeterminate (e.g. `working…`). | Layouts: `.dv-wide` puts plate and words side by side from 860 px. `.dv-small` makes the plate a thumbnail beside a line. Without either, they stack. ## Theming Uses `--ink`, `--ink-2`, `--ink-3`, `--accent` (the readout at 100%), `--serif`, `--sans`. | Variable | Default | | |---|---|---| | `--dv-plate` | `min(100%, 520px)` | The plate's width. | | `--dv-size` | `clamp(44px, 12cqi, 88px)` | The readout. | | `--dv-gap` | `clamp(18px, 5cqi, 48px)` | Between plate and words. | ## Accessibility The `` is labelled by its `

# Pick note: sf-loader, 2026-11-03

## The hunt

About 450 candidates across 14 contact sheets: Wikimedia Commons (including the Met, LoC, Rijksmuseum, Polona, Houghton,
Chester Beatty and Freer files mirrored there), the Art Institute of Chicago and the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access
APIs. The Met's own API refused us (403, then 410), so its files came through Commons.

Sheets, all in `tools/engine/jobs/`:

- `loader-hunt-a/hunt/sheet.png`: Utamaro sericulture, charkha, norias, al-Jazari, abacus, cash coins
- `loader-hunt-b/hunt/sheet.png`: Gengzhi tu, Utamaro (LoC), Books of Hours, Kehar Singh, prayer wheels
- `loader-hunt-mus1/sheet.jpg`, `loader-hunt-mus2/sheet.jpg`, `loader-hunt-mus4/sheet.jpg`: AIC and Cleveland. Spinning,
  reeling, beads, spindles, the whole Utamaro and Shunsho sericulture series, and the Cleveland *Sericulture* handscroll
- `loader-hunt-d`, `-e`, `-i` (`hunt/sheet.png`): astrolabes, retes, plates, the Met and Louvre astrolabes
- `loader-hunt-g/hunt/sheet.png`: al-Jazari water-raising and clock folios, Hokusai's *Waterwheel at Onden*,
  Agricola, Ramelli, the bookwheel
- `loader-hunt-j/hunt/sheet.png`: Japanese sericulture prints (LoC, NDL)
- `loader-hunt-k/hunt/sheet.png`: every page of Apian's *Astronomicum Caesareum* (Polona, Houghton, the Met)

Shortlist sheet: `tools/engine/jobs/loader-shortlist.jpg`.

## Shortlist

1. **Apian, the lunar dragon volvelle (Draco), *Astronomicum Caesareum*, Ingolstadt 1540**, hand-coloured woodcut,
   National Library of Poland (Polona) copy, public domain, 8822 × 11649 (used at 3840). **Picked.**
2. Apian, the sky volvelle (star map), same copy. Glorious, but its disc is all small constellation figures, and the
   real silk thread lies loose across it.
3. Apian, the twelve-headed dragon of the nodes (Houghton copy). A curled, browned page at 4031 px.
4. *Sericulture*, Southern Song handscroll after Lou Shou, Cleveland 1977.5, CC0. A girl winding quills at a spoked
   wheel beside a creel of bobbins. Beautiful, but the wheel is about 90 px across in a 25,776 px scan: too small to handle.
5. The same scroll's reeling frame over the cocoon basin. Drawn at an angle, so it can't turn honestly.
6. Kehar Singh, *Weaving and Spinning*, Punjab c. 1860. The charkha is nearly edge-on.
7. Utamaro, *Women Engaged in the Sericulture Industry* No. 9 (reeling). The reel is oblique and half-hidden by the figure.
8. al-Jazari, *Waterwheel worked by donkey power*, Met 1315. Its gears are painted as edge-on lenses, and it's the
   clock's own manuscript again.
9. al-Jazari, water clock with an arch of twelve roundels, Freer 1354. The roundels would have to change colour, which
   means painting them.
10. Islamic astrolabes (Louvre, AIC, Harvard). Turning the rete means inventing the plate under it, and no collection
    photographs the parts apart, face-on, at this quality.
11. Chassignet's copper rete (BnF). A rete with no plate.
12. Yoshifuji, *Ito zukuri* (LoC, 7835 px). The reel is cut by the sheet edge and drawn side-on.

## Why the dragon

- It is a real machine made of paper. Apian coloured, cut and assembled the instruments in his own workshop. On this
  plate one paper disc turns on a pin over the printed mater (the base, with the zodiac). The disc carries the dragon,
  the two tabs CAPVT and CAVDA, rings of year marks and the arched latitude scales. Turning that disc, pixel for pixel,
  is exactly what the book's reader did. Because the disc is a full circle, turning it never uncovers any of the mater.
- It goes round, and it advances in proportion. The dragon's head marks the moon's ascending node, and the nodes regress
  steadily backwards through the zodiac, one full turn in about 18.6 years. A determinate job turns it in proportion
  against the mater's real graduated ring. A job with no value just keeps it going round.
- It is sharp. The woodcut hatching holds at 3840 px (engine inspect: no enlargement), and the hand colour is crisp.
- It can be handled. You can take the disc and turn it, the way the reader set it from the tables.
- One culture, one craft: Renaissance German astronomy and printing, for Charles V.
